It's not actually a "head transplant" though, is it?

This person is receiving a transplant. The person who's receiving the transplant is contained in the head, so the head is actually the thing that's receiving the transplant. The thing that's being transplanted is a body. So it's actually a "body transplant."

Seems that way to me at least. For whatever that's worth...

For me a "body transplant" would be implanting a brain in a complete body. Head transplant would be removing a head and placing it on the neck-down portion of another body. I think it's really just semantics though.

Technically still a head transplant since the head is the thing being removed and attached I believe.

But since he is transplanting his head to escape the disease destroying his body, I would consider it a body transplant, whereas if somebody was transplanting their brain into another skull because of some medical problem with their head, I'd call that a head transplant, but I'm not a doctor so nobody cares what I would call it. Plus it sounds way cooler to call it a head transplant.

I'd agree that it sounds cooler to call it a head transplant. It's also easier for people to grasp, just because, as you say, the head is the thing being removed and reattached.

Still though - I think that technically that's not what it is, since underlying all of it is the fact that it's a person who's receiving the transplant, and the person receiving the transplant is the person who's inside that head. The transplant the person inside that head is receiving is of an entire body.

I doubt it'll ever be referred to that way, and it's not as if I'm demanding that it be. It makes no real difference to me. It's just a sort of philosophical point that I thought of the first time I saw one of these headlines, and decided to post about this time.

I think it's going to be one of those things that never really gets an answer because both sides have pretty equal footing and it makes little difference beyond bureaucratic consistency, but it's definitely still something interesting to think about.

Just with my very limited medical knowledge and from what little information I've gathered about the history of this procedure, this man will almost certainly die. If not from infection, from rejection or other complications we hadn't even thought of yet. Even if it is a success, I can't imagine it will go off without a hitch, with my best case prediction being a relatively normal life with significant complications and lots of outpatient treatment, and my worst case (besides death) being that he ends up literally going insane because of incompatibilities in his brain with the new body.

But then again, I'm not a doctor in the least so I could be completely wrong. This will definitely be one for the history books if they go through with it though and there's tons to be learned from it, so I applaud this man for his bravery and contribution to medical science, and I have my fingers crossed for him.
